title: Week 35 Analysis
commentary:
The tracker resumes after a three-month gap. Collection stopped at the end of May and restarted this week, so the interval between this entry and the last one reflects a failure of the instrument rather than a quiet period in the field. Readers comparing week 22 to week 35 should treat the intervening months as unsampled rather than empty. The corpus now holds 259 cases, of which 41 are academic.

Everything added this week came from the research literature — fourteen items across PubMed, arXiv and Semantic Scholar, and no media reports at all. That is partly an artefact of a tightened relevance filter and partly a real feature of where the subject currently sits: the academic response to the past year of reporting is now arriving in volume. The most consequential single item is a case report, “You're Not Crazy”: A Case of New-onset AI-associated Psychosis, which is the kind of documentation that has been conspicuously scarce. Alongside it, a scoping review of the mental health harms of LLM-based chatbots and a paper asking directly whether interacting with artificial intelligence causes delusions suggest the question has moved from journalism into clinical literature where it can be argued about properly.

The more interesting shift is from description to mechanism. Three of this week's preprints examine how the behaviour arises rather than that it occurs: one measures how sycophancy intensifies when a conversation carries emotional weight, one traces four distinct trajectories in how models respond to a user's escalating delusional claims, and a third finds longitudinal evidence that general-purpose chatbots actively encourage relational engagement rather than merely tolerating it. If those findings hold, they point at design choices rather than at unusually vulnerable users, which is a materially different problem and a more tractable one.

The underlying distribution has not moved. Reality distortion accounts for 35 per cent of media cases and romantic attachment for 28, together still close to two-thirds of the corpus, as they were in May. That stability is worth noting mainly because it is unremarkable: three months passed, the collection method changed substantially, and the shape of the material did not. As always, these counts measure what is being reported and indexed, not how often the underlying harm occurs, and this week's academic-only intake should not be read as a decline in media coverage — the media side of this window is simply under-sampled.

spotlight.title: “You're Not Crazy”: A Case of New-onset AI-associated Psychosis
spotlight.context: A single documented case report in Innovations in Clinical Neuroscience — the form of evidence this subject has most conspicuously lacked. Most of the corpus is journalism describing events at second hand; a clinical write-up can be examined, contested and built on. One case establishes nothing about prevalence, but it moves the question into a literature equipped to answer it.
